claim: The synthetic division rate is deliberately inflated roughly 15.7x over the real rate, so any loss trained on it needs reweighting before its priors are calibrated.
source: topic 732103 post 3507381 by Jose Freitas Alves Neto
quote: The division rate is deliberately inflated (4.07% of nodes vs ~0.26% in reality). A model starved of examples never learns mitosis. Re-weight your loss by the real rate if you need calibrated priors.

claim: The author concedes the synthetic data's weakest axes are exactly nucleus texture and contrast, i.e. the appearance channel a detector trains on.
source: topic 732103 post 3507381 by Jose Freitas Alves Neto
quote: Distribution match is partial. Nucleus texture and contrast are the weakest axes. The value here is the labels — density, lineage and mitosis — much more than photorealism.

claim: A subtle synthetic-data trap: both daughters inherit the parent's track_id, so nodes[:,4] is a lineage/clone id and is NOT unique per track after a division.
source: topic 732103 post 3521156 by Jose Freitas Alves Neto
quote: both daughters inherit the parent's track_id. So nodes[:, 4] is a lineage/clone id, not a unique track — after a division, two distinct tracks share it. ... If you build your candidate graph off track_id expecting uniqueness, it will look like cells teleport.

claim: THE SINGLE MOST DANGEROUS DEFECT: in 6bba_fc516dc6 the volumes at t=81 and t=82 are byte-identical yet the GT edge moves 8.90 um - larger than the 7 um matching radius - so copying a detection across a frozen frame is guaranteed to miss.

claim: The 8.90 um frozen-frame jump is almost entirely in Z (23->18 voxels = 8.125 um of the 8.90), i.e. it is an annotation wobble along the 4x-anisotropic axis on one elongated nucleus, not real motion.
quote: show_crops(22, 81, 24) vs show_crops(22, 82, 24): XY panels and the red centroid are visually unchanged; only the XZ/YZ red dot shifts. plt.scatter(169,175); plt.scatter(161,179); plt.imshow(img[82,18]) shows BOTH points on one elongated blob.

claim: The frozen-frame GT wobble is not a one-off: only one cell in that frame moved, and the cell is elongated with a Z-span over 15 voxels, so even a perfectly centred prediction cannot cover both annotations within 7 um.

CHUNKING TRAP: chunks are one full timepoint (1,64,256,256), so a time-major read touches one chunk while reading one Z-slice across all time touches 100 chunks - 100x the I/O for 64x less data.
source: topic 734053 post 3510828 by maximo lorenzo y losada
quote: Zarr decompresses a whole chunk regardless of how little you asked for, so reading one full timepoint touches 1 chunk while reading a single Z-slice across all time touches 100 chunks - 100x the I/O for 64x less data. Time-major access is nearly free

claim: INTENSITY TRAP: the shipped quantiles are 0.0->15, 0.1->75, 0.9->497, 0.99->1478, 1.0->4319, so naive min-max scaling puts 90% of voxels below 0.112 of the range; clip at the 99th percentile first.
source: topic 734053 post 3510828 by maximo lorenzo y losada
quote: 0.0 -> 15, 0.1 -> 75, 0.9 -> 497, 0.99 -> 1478, 1.0 -> 4319 The range is 15 to 4319, but 90% of voxels sit at or below 497, which is 11.2% of that range. Min-max scaling to [0,1] therefore puts 90% of your data below 0.112.

claim: ANISOTROPY TRAP quantified: Z/Y is exactly 4.0, so two detections 4 voxels apart in Z are 6.5 um apart while 4 voxels apart in Y are 1.63 um - any gating radius computed on raw voxel indices understates Z by 4x.
source: topic 734053 post 3510828 by maximo lorenzo y losada
quote: So Z / Y = exactly 4.0 - one voxel step in Z covers four times the physical distance of one step in Y or X. ... Two detections 4 voxels apart in Z are 6.5 micrometers apart; 4 voxels apart in Y are 1.63.
